key_findings: Romanian dissection + MRI study. 'The anterior divisions of the S2, S3 and S4 spinal nerves give rise to the pudendal nerve.' 'This nerve, together with the internal pudendal artery, are closely associated with the rigid superior border of the sacrospinous ligament, actually passing between the piriformis muscle and the sacrospinous ligament and then between the ligament and the upper border of the sciatic spine.' 'The elements of the internal pudendal neurovascular bundle follow their extrapelvic course surrounding the ischial spine in the deep gluteal region in order to reenter the pelvis through the lesser sciatic notch.'
clinical_relevance: Shows the interligamentous (sacrospinous-sacrotuberous) segment - the commonest entrapment site - and the transgluteal landmark (ischial spine) used for pudendal block and decompression.

key_findings: Retrospective series of 'bilateral PND' in 74 women. 'When bilateral PND was the only procedure done to treat the symptoms, the cure rates of perineodynia, anal incontinence and urinary incontinence were 8/14, 4/5 and 3/5, respectively.' Anatomy as stated by the authors: 'In the canal the nerve crosses the sharp edge of the sacro-tuberous ligament (falciform process)'. Shafik trans-perineal technique: 'Vertical incision of the skin between the anus and the ischial tuberosity.- Opening of the ischio-rectal fossa with scissors.- The inferior rectal nerve is hooked under the finger and followed to the entrance of the Alcock's canal'.
clinical_relevance: Pudendal canal syndrome (entrapment) and trans-perineal (Shafik) decompression via the ischioanal fossa; the inferior rectal nerve is the guide to the canal entrance.
notes: Small (347x287) video-still; use at half-slide. Companion Fig 4 (view from below) was rejected - nerve not identifiable with confidence. Only cadaver figure in our set that is centred on the opened canal itself; also the only OA source here mentioning the falciform process.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Skeletal muscles of the pelvic outlet in women. The skeletal muscles of the pelvic outlet share muscle bundles and are continuous, forming a continuous skeletal muscle sheet. A The pelvic outlet muscles in women from the medial aspect. key_findings: 26 formalin-embalmed cadavers (16 M, 10 F), 52 hemipelves. 'In the present study, 27 out of 52 hemipelves (51.9%) were identified as type I having a single pudendal nerve trunk'. Type IIa: 'This branching pattern was observed in 7 out of 52 hemipelves (13.5%).' 'Twelve out of 52 hemipelves (23.1%) were type IIb ... but the inferior rectal nerve did not pass through the sacrospinous ligament.' 'Three trunked pudendal nerve (type III) was observed in 11.5% of hemipelves. In 14/52 hemipelves (26.9%), communication with the sciatic nerve was noted'. Literature (Mahakkanukrauh 2005, 73 nerves): 'type I is defined as one-trunked (41/73; 56.2%) ... type III is two-trunked with one trunk as an inferior rectal nerve piercing through the sacrospinous ligament (8/73; 11%) ... type V is three-trunked (9/73;12.3%)'.
clinical_relevance: Multiple trunks / an inferior rectal nerve piercing the sacrospinous ligament matter for sacrospinous colpopexy, transgluteal pudendal block (incomplete block) and decompression surgery.
notes: CC BY (Cureus). The Abstract erroneously writes 'inferior gluteal nerve' for types IIa/IIb; the Results body and captions say 'inferior rectal nerve' - quote the body. The table of earlier studies gives the Mahakkanukrauh classification (requested 'Mahakkanukrauh type' data). i02/i05/i07 (sciatic-communication subtypes) downloaded and deleted (redundant).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Sagittal section of the pelvis showing the sectional views of rectum, canal, urinary bladder, prostate, and the pubis. (AOP: artery of penis, BP: bulb of penis, DEP: deep artery of the penis, DOA: dorsal artery of the penis, and RCP: right crus of the penis.)
figures.specimen: human cadaver (male), median sagittal hemisection of pelvis
figures.what_it_shows: The intrapelvic artery of the penis descends below the puboprostatic ligaments behind the pubic symphysis and divides into the dorsal and deep arteries of the penis near the bulb and right crus.
figures.labels_visible_in_image: Rectum, Urinary bladder, AOP, Pubis, Prostate, DOA, DEP, RCP, Anal canal, BP

key_findings: Case report. 'The artery of the penis arose from a common arterial trunk from the left internal iliac artery.' 'The artery of the penis coursed forwards between the bladder and lateral pelvic wall until the pubis. Thereafter it passed below the puboprostatic ligaments and divided into deep and dorsal arteries of the penis just behind the lower border of the pubic symphysis'. 'The left internal pudendal artery was reduced in size and it supplied the musculature of the perineum and the anal canal. It also supplied the bulb of the penis.'
clinical_relevance: Such intrapelvic penile supply runs near the prostate/puboprostatic ligaments - at risk in radical prostatectomy; relevant to erectile dysfunction and penile revascularisation.
notes: CC BY. The authors do NOT use the term 'accessory pudendal artery'; the slide may say 'aksesuar pudendal arter ile aynı paternde' but must not attribute the term to them. Fig 2 is a sagittally hemisected pelvis (gross specimen, not a cross-sectional image series).
